summary:
Moon Analog Finder helps mission planners identify Earth locations that can serve as test analogs for specific environments near the lunar south pole.

A user selects a lunar south-polar location and a testing purpose, such as rover mobility, shadow operations, or darkness survival. The tool uses NASA lunar datasets to characterize that target and compares its relevant terrain and environmental properties against a large library of Earth candidate windows. Rather than claiming that any Earth location “is like the Moon,” the tool produces explainable, factor-level similarity scores and identifies where each analogy is useful and where it breaks down.

The result is an interactive, data-driven way to move from “Where on Earth should we test for this lunar environment?” to a ranked, inspectable set of candidate sites.
details:
Every Moon base test starts on Earth. Choosing where should not be guesswork.

Teams preparing for the lunar south pole keep returning to the same short list of analog sites, chosen by reputation. No tool answers the planner’s real question: for this lunar spot and this test, where on Earth should I go, and what will a test there fail to prove?

Moon Analog Finder answers it in three clicks

Click 1: Where on the Moon?

Choose a lunar south-polar target. Click anywhere between 80°S and 90°S, or select a named lunar region. The selected area becomes the lunar reference environment.

Click 2: What are we testing?

Choose the operational purpose. Select rover mobility, shadow operations, or darkness survival. Different purposes emphasize different environmental characteristics, so there is no single universally “best” Earth analog.

Click 3: Where on Earth?

Inspect the ranked terrestrial candidates. Moon Analog Finder compares the lunar target with Earth candidate windows and returns factor-level similarity scores, supporting data, and limitations for the strongest matches.

What the challenge asked for, and what we built

  • Go beyond visual similarity. Every match is measured: slope, roughness across scales, sunlight, darkness, temperature, frozen ground. The 3D view never appears without the scores.
  • Say where the analogy breaks. Every site has a “where it breaks” line. Gravity, vacuum and radiation are always shown as not matchable.
  • Look beyond the well-known sites. The whole Earth is searched. Known analog sites are shown separately from new candidates.
  • Consider scale. 10 km squares placed every 2.5 km. A finer 2 km stage was built, tested and dropped because it did not help.
  • Connect to exploration. Each test purpose follows a need NASA has published for south pole operations. The weights and cut-offs are ours.
  • Search systematically. One similarity metric, open code, a published benchmark.
  • Make it usable. Limit the search by country, distance from a base or altitude, or type in a site you already use to see how it scores.

What is different about our approach

Existing analog research often begins with known terrestrial sites and asks what planetary conditions those sites can represent. Moon Analog Finder reverses that workflow: start with a specific lunar south-polar target and an operational testing need, then search Earth systematically for locations with useful matching characteristics.

The project's contribution is therefore not a claim that every surfaced Earth location is a newly discovered planetary analog. Rather, the tool provides a reproducible method for surfacing and comparing candidate analog locations from the requirements of a particular lunar environment.

It finds what experts found, without being told

  • Mauna Kea, Hawaii, came out first among sites below 3,500 m for de Gerlache Rim 2 terrain.
  • The Antarctic Dry Valleys ranked third among sites below 3,500 m for Malapert Massif terrain.
  • Our shadow model reproduces NASA’s lunar sunlight map within 1.5 percentage points on average, and its permanent shadow map within 1.2.

What it found

  • Arctic Canada (64.30 N, 66.14 W), for the IM-2 landing site. Terrain match 0.97. Median slope 5.1 degrees on both bodies, shadow share within 4 percentage points, the same drivable ground and line of sight. 131 km from Iqaluit, and in November the Sun sits in the lunar range for about 6 hours a day.
  • Mauna Kea, Hawaii (19.84 N, 155.52 W), for de Gerlache Rim 2. Terrain match 0.87, shadow share within 3 percentage points, 26 km from the nearest town.
  • North Greenland (80.07 N, 23.37 W), for ice drilling at Haworth. Ground frozen all year on both bodies, slopes of 2.7 against 2.6 degrees.
  • Malapert Massif has no easy answer. The only strong match on Earth is in the Andes at 5,700 m (28.02 S, 68.75 W). Below 3,500 m the best is a partial match in north Greenland. Knowing that is a result too.

Full list with every number: docs/CANDIDATES.md in the repository.

It tells you how far to trust it

Every score carries a measured error. We split 2,629 lunar squares in half and asked the method to find each half’s partner among all the others: it ranks the true partner in the top 1% half of the time, against 1% by chance. From that test, 0.87 and above means “same kind of terrain” and below 0.80 means no evidence of similarity. Moving a square by 2.5 km changes a score by about 0.06, so sites closer than that are shown as tied.

Against 21 known lunar analog sites, the terrain score beats random bare land 61 to 65% of the time, where chance is 50%. It recognises broad landscapes like the Atacama and misses single-feature sites like Meteor Crater. So we call it a terrain screen, not a validated analog finder, and no candidate has been field-checked. Rock type, dust and access are not covered. A planner can only use a tool whose limits are known.

Who it helps

  • Field-test planners get options beyond the usual sites, with the reason each one fits and what a test there cannot prove.
  • Simulation teams get open terrain models that match specific lunar regions.
  • Anyone can use it: one link, no login, open data and open code.

Built with

Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, FastAPI), JavaScript (Leaflet, three.js) and Modal for the Earth scan, scoring service and hosting. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with research, planning and code. Every score comes from the data and code in the repository, not from an AI model. The demo video uses real app footage; its motion graphics and music were made with AI assistance. This is an independent project, not a NASA product.

View Project Source here: https://github.com/shashi0d/moon-analog-finder
